title: Acute Myeloid Leukemia
subject: Pathology
summary: AML is a clonal proliferation of myeloid blasts in marrow and blood, often driven by specific cytogenetic abnormalities. It presents with cytopenias, bleeding and infections, and requires rapid diagnosis and cytotoxic therapy.

sections.p: AML is defined by ≥20 % myeloid blasts in bone marrow or peripheral blood. Diagnosis combines morphology, immunophenotype and cytogenetics.
b: Myeloid blasts: 3–5 nucleoli, fine azurophilic granules
Auer rods: characteristic red‑staining rods in promyelocytes

t.b: Markers: CD13, CD33, CD117, MPO positive; CD34, HLA‑DR variable
t(15;17) PML‑RARA, t(8;21) RUNX1‑RUNX1T1, inv(16) CBFB‑MYH11

sections.p: Risk stratification uses cytogenetics, molecular markers and age. The ELN 2022 risk groups (favorable, intermediate, adverse) guide therapy intensity.
In low‑resource settings, preceding infections, HIV, malaria, and prior MDS or chemotherapy are common precipitating factors.
Patients often have fatigue, pallor, bruising, petechiae, and recurrent infections. Splenomegaly and lymphadenopathy may occur.
Work‑up focuses on confirming blasts, ruling out ALL, and identifying cytogenetic risk.

t.b: PT, aPTT prolonged, fibrinogen low, D-dimer high

sections.p: Early complications include DIC, leukostasis, severe infections and organ infiltration.
b: Differentiation syndrome in APL: fever, dyspnea, pulmonary oedema

sections.p: Treat the underlying cause, provide supportive care, and initiate cytotoxic induction. APL requires immediate all-trans retinoic acid.
b: Avoid drugs that prolong QT or cause myelosuppression in resource‑limited settings

t.b: Avoid in patients with severe hepatic dysfunction

sections.p: Post‑remission maintenance, regular marrow exams, and infection prophylaxis are essential. Prevention focuses on early detection of pre‑leukemic states.
b: Screen for HIV and treat promptly

sections.p: AML can mimic ALL, myelodysplastic syndromes and severe infections.
b: Severe infection – fever and cytopenias but no blasts

sections.p: Low blast counts may be missed on peripheral smear; cytogenetic tests may be unavailable, delaying risk stratification.
b: Coagulation abnormalities may be subtle early in DIC

whenToSeekHelp: Signs of DIC (purpura, petechiae, low fibrinogen)

faq.q: How do you differentiate AML from ALL on a blood film?
faq.a: AML shows myeloid blasts with Auer rods and fine granules; ALL shows lymphoblasts with scant cytoplasm and no granules.

faq.q: What is the first drug used in acute promyelocytic leukaemia?
faq.a: All‑trans retinoic acid, which induces differentiation of promyelocytes.

faq.q: Why is cytarabine combined with an anthracycline in induction?
faq.a: Cytarabine kills proliferating blasts; anthracycline adds cytotoxicity and improves remission rates.

exam: A 45‑year‑old man presents with fatigue and bruising. CBC shows 12 × 10⁹/L neutrophils, 5 × 10⁹/L platelets, 2 × 10⁹/L blasts. What is the next best step? — Perform a peripheral smear to confirm blasts and order flow cytometry for immunophenotyping.
A patient with suspected AML has a normal karyotype but NPM1 mutation. What is his risk category? — Intermediate risk; consider standard induction followed by consolidation.
During induction, a patient develops fever, dyspnea, and pulmonary infiltrates. What complication is most likely? — Leukostasis; give urgent cytoreduction with hydroxyurea.

A 30‑year‑old woman with HIV presents with anemia and thrombocytopenia. Peripheral smear shows Auer rods. What is the most likely diagnosis? — AML, likely secondary to HIV‑associated marrow dysregulation.
A patient with AML develops sudden hypotension and purpura. What is the most urgent management? — Treat DIC: give fresh frozen plasma, cryoprecipitate, and platelet transfusions.

A 50‑year‑old man with AML is started on induction. He develops fever, rigors, and pulmonary oedema. What syndrome is this? — Differentiation syndrome; treat with dexamethasone and discontinue the offending agent.
A patient with AML has a t(15;17) translocation. What targeted therapy should be started immediately? — All‑trans retinoic acid, possibly with arsenic trioxide.
A patient with AML is in a rural clinic with no cytogenetics available. How should you risk‑stratify? — Use morphology and flow cytometry; treat as intermediate risk pending further testing.
